teaser: Painted for a Spanish palace, starring a horse he never rode over that pass.
review_notes:
First version (this one, Malmaison): commissioned by Charles IV of Spain for the Royal Palace in Madrid, painted 1800 to 1801, about 261 x 221 cm.
Crossing of the Great St Bernard Pass in May 1800 with roughly 40,000 men; Battle of Marengo 14 June 1800.
Napoleon's refusal to pose and his wish to be shown calm on a spirited horse are reported by David's early biographers; paraphrased, not quoted.
Uniform and hat from Marengo lent to David and an assistant posing on a ladder: traditional account.
Five versions between 1801 and 1805 (Malmaison, Charlottenburg, two at Versailles, Belvedere Vienna).
Signature on the horse's chest strap reads L. DAVID with the Revolutionary year IX; faint at this resolution.
Joseph Bonaparte took the painting from Madrid, later kept it at Point Breeze, Bordentown, New Jersey; it reached Malmaison in 1949 through a descendant's bequest.
Delaroche's mule version dated 1850.
Charlemagne's crossing dated 773, Hannibal's 218 BC.

lesson.text: This canvas was ordered for a wall in Madrid. In 1800 the king of Spain, Charles IV, wanted a portrait of France's new ruler for his Royal Palace, where it would join a gallery of great commanders. So the first viewers David had in mind were foreign courtiers who needed to be impressed.

The subject was fresh news. In May 1800, Napoleon Bonaparte, thirty years old and First Consul of France, led some 40,000 men over the Great St Bernard Pass, high in the Alps, to surprise the Austrian army in Italy. A month later he beat them at Marengo.
Napoleon did not cross on a rearing stallion. He followed his troops a few days later, in fair weather, on a mule led by a local guide. A mule is slower and far safer on a mountain path.

He also refused to pose. A likeness did not matter, he told David; what mattered was the character. His one instruction was to be shown calm on a fiery horse. David borrowed the uniform and hat worn at Marengo and had an assistant model them, perched on top of a ladder.

lesson.title: Calm on a fiery horse
lesson.text: David turned that one sentence into four details.

spots.title: The face
spots.text: Smooth, pale, turned toward you. Not a hair is out of place under the two-cornered hat. He seems to be sitting for a portrait, not riding up a cliff.

spots.title: The horse
spots.text: Now the animal: a rolling eye, flared nostrils, an open mouth showing teeth, ears back. All the fear in the picture belongs to the horse.

spots.title: The bare hand
spots.text: The right hand, ungloved, points up and forward, beyond the edge of the canvas. The goal is somewhere you cannot see.

spots.title: The gloved hand
spots.text: The left hand, in a white glove, holds the reins loosely against the mane. One hand is enough to control a panicking stallion.

lesson.text: Put the two halves together and you get the message. France had lived through ten years of revolution, terror and war. Here is the man who rides that wild energy without effort. The horse stands in for the country, and for history itself.
This is a portrait of an idea, not of an event. David shows what Napoleon wanted people to believe about him: perfect calm in the middle of chaos.

A message this simple needs a simple design. David trained in Rome and admired ancient sculpture, and he built pictures the way a mason builds a wall: a few strong lines first, everything else hung on them.
Almost everything here leans the same way.

lines.label: The horse
lines.text: From rump to muzzle, the animal's body makes one long diagonal that climbs from lower right to upper left.

lines.label: The arm
lines.text: The pointing arm repeats that slope higher up, like a second arrow laid over the first.

lines.label: The mountain
lines.text: The dark ridge runs the other way, falling from left to right. Rider and ground form a big X, which is why the horse seems to burst upward.

lesson.text: Even the weather cooperates. The cloak, the mane and the tail all blow forward, in the direction of the pointing hand. A wind that strong should be in his face on a mountain pass. David puts it at his back, as if nature itself were pushing him to Italy.

David and his studio painted five versions between 1801 and 1805. You can tell them apart by color. Here the cloak is golden yellow and the horse is white with dark patches. In the later ones the cloak turns red.
At the bottom left, the snow has been swept off a few slabs of rock. David carved a history lesson into them, in capital letters.
Whose name is cut into the rock in the largest letters?

spots.title: BONAPARTE
spots.text: His name sits on top, in the cleanest letters. Under it, half cut off by the frame, you can read ANNIBAL and, further right, KAROLUS MAGNUS.

lesson.text: Hannibal took his army and its elephants over the Alps in 218 BC to attack Rome. Charlemagne, Karolus Magnus in Latin, crossed in 773 to conquer northern Italy. Napoleon's name is added to the list, above the others. At that date he had ruled France for barely six months.

The painter knew something about power. Jacques-Louis David had been a radical during the Revolution, voted for the death of Louis XVI, and went to prison when his political friends fell. His style, called Neoclassicism, copies the clear outlines and smooth, hard surfaces of ancient statues. You cannot see a single brushstroke.
That polish makes the hero look carved. It also lets David tuck the real army into the gaps around the horse, small, bent and nearly the color of the rock.

spots.title: A cannon wheel
spots.text: Under the horse's belly a gun carriage is being dragged uphill. Hauling the artillery over the pass was the truly hard part of the crossing.

spots.title: The soldiers
spots.text: Men in blue coats and cocked hats trudge up the slope with their backs to you. Nobody painted their portraits.

spots.title: The strap
spots.text: The dark strap across the horse's chest carries David's signature and the date in the Revolutionary calendar, year nine. The artist signs on the harness.

spots.title: The flag
spots.text: At the right edge, a scrap of red, white and blue: the tricolor, far below, carried by troops still climbing.

spots.title: The cloak
spots.text: The cloak flares into a great curl above the horse's head, almost a wing. It is the brightest patch of color on the canvas.

spots.title: The tail
spots.text: The long tail streams forward between the hind legs, blown the same way as the cloak.

spots.title: Sword and sash
spots.text: A curved saber hangs at his hip under a fringed sash. It stays sheathed. Up here he commands by pointing.

lesson.text: The Madrid wall did not keep its picture long. In 1808 Napoleon put his brother Joseph on the Spanish throne. When Joseph fled five years later, he took the canvas with him, and eventually hung it in his house in New Jersey. A descendant left it in 1949 to Malmaison, the home near Paris where Napoleon lived at the time of the crossing.

In 1850 the painter Paul Delaroche produced his own version of the crossing: a tired man in a gray coat, hunched on a mule, led by a guide through the snow. It is closer to the facts, and far less famous.
Everyone who reads about this picture learns about the mule. And still, when you think of Napoleon in the Alps, which image comes to mind?

quiz.question: Who commissioned this first version of the painting?
options: The king of Spain, Charles IV
quiz.explanation: Charles IV ordered it for the Royal Palace in Madrid.

quiz.question: How did Napoleon actually cross the pass?
options: On a mule led by a guide
On the white horse shown here
quiz.explanation: He followed his troops a few days later on a mule.

quiz.question: What was Napoleon's one instruction to David?
options: To show him calm on a fiery horse
quiz.explanation: That contrast between calm rider and frightened horse carries the whole message.

quiz.question: Which names are carved in the rocks next to BONAPARTE?
quiz.explanation: Both crossed the Alps with armies before Napoleon.

quiz.question: In which direction does the wind blow in the painting?
quiz.explanation: Cloak, mane and tail are all blown forward, as if nature were pushing him on.

quiz.question: Where did David place his signature?
options: On the rock at lower left
On the strap across the horse's chest
quiz.explanation: The strap carries his name and the Revolutionary year nine.

facts.text: Napoleon posed for David for many hours for this portrait.
facts.explanation: He refused to pose; an assistant modeled the borrowed uniform on a ladder.

facts.text: David and his studio made five versions of this painting.
facts.explanation: They were painted between 1801 and 1805 and differ in the colors of cloak and horse.

facts.text: The painting has always stayed in Europe.
facts.explanation: Joseph Bonaparte hung it for a time in his house in New Jersey.
